blocks.h: On completing this chapter, the reader should be able to:

items.h: Explain the governance structure of a Nigerian life insurance company under NIIRA 2025, including the Board of Directors’ composition and fit-and-proper requirements, the role of the MD/CEO, and the function of the Executive Committee.

Describe the mandate, core activities, key outputs, and principal internal relationships of each of the twelve core departments of a life insurance company: Actuarial and Risk, Underwriting, Claims, Sales and Distribution, Marketing and Communications, Operations and Technology, Finance and Investment, Legal and Compliance, Human Resources, Customer Experience, Strategy and Research, and Internal Audit.

Explain the three lines of defence model as applied to a Nigerian life insurer, and identify the specific roles of the first, second, and third lines in the governance and risk management framework required by NIIRA 2025.

Describe the recommended organisational structure for three distinct company size profiles (the start-up insurer, the mid-size established player, and the large composite) explaining how reporting lines, spans of control, and departmental boundaries should differ across each profile.

Explain the distinction between functional and matrix organisational structures, and evaluate the merits and limitations of each in the Nigerian life insurance context, particularly for insurers operating across multiple distribution channels or product lines.

Describe the critical interdepartmental integration points in a life insurance company: the underwriting-claims interface, the sales-actuarial dialogue, the marketing-product development alignment, and the technology-operations partnership.

Identify and describe the key governance documents that underpin a well-governed Nigerian life insurer: the Board Charter, the Delegation of Authority, the Conflict of Interest Policy, and the Code of Conduct.

Explain the NIIRA 2025 requirements for the appointment of key management personnel, including the Chief Actuary, the Chief Risk Officer, the Chief Compliance Officer, and the Internal Audit Head, and describe the accountability structure for each role.

Describe the governance and reporting obligations of the Board’s principal committees (the Audit Committee, the Risk Committee, the Investment Committee, and the Remuneration Committee) and explain how these committees interface with management.

Apply the organisational design principles in this chapter to evaluate a real or hypothetical Nigerian life insurer’s structure and identify specific improvements aligned with NIIRA 2025 governance requirements and best-practice insurance management.

blocks.h: A life insurance company’s organisational structure is not an administrative convenience. It is a strategic decision that determines how fast the company makes decisions, how clearly accountability is assigned, how effectively risk is identified and managed, and how well the company can execute its strategy. An insurer with a brilliant strategy but a poorly designed organisation will execute that strategy badly. An insurer with a well-designed organisation that enables fast, accountable, and technically informed decision-making can execute even a modest strategy effectively.

This is particularly true for Nigerian life insurers navigating the post-NIIRA 2025 environment. The reform Act imposes new governance requirements (Board composition, fit-and-proper standards, three lines of defence, actuarial and risk function mandates) that must be embedded in the organisation’s structure, not merely noted in a compliance document. An insurer that places its Chief Risk Officer three levels below the CEO, gives its Internal Audit function no direct Board access, and combines its Compliance and Legal functions under a single over-stretched manager is not merely under-resourced; it is structurally non-compliant with NIIRA 2025.

Part Seven of this book addresses the life insurance company as an organisational subject in its own right. This chapter addresses the macro-level governance structure, the twelve core departments and their mandates, the integration between departments, the governance documents that formalise the structure, and the recommended structures for companies at different stages of scale. Chapter 35 addresses the people within the structure, human capital, professional development, and culture. Chapter 36 addresses the information infrastructure that enables strategic decision-making, research, data, and competitive intelligence.

blocks.text: 34.2 Governance Structure: Board, MD/CEO, and Executive Committee

blocks.h: The Board of Directors is the apex governance body of the life insurance company. It is accountable to shareholders for the oversight of the company’s strategy, risk management, financial performance, and regulatory compliance. The Board’s authority is supreme within the governance framework: the MD/CEO and all members of management are accountable to the Board, not the reverse.
NIIRA 2025 sets specific requirements for the composition and conduct of the Boards of licensed insurance companies:

items.h: Minimum size: A minimum of five directors. The majority must be non-executive directors, ensuring independent oversight of management.

Independent directors: At least two truly independent non-executive directors (individuals with no material relationship to the company, its major shareholders, or its management) must be on the Board. Independent directors chair the Audit and Risk Committees.

Fit and proper standard: Every director must meet NAICOM’s fit and proper requirements: adequate educational qualifications or professional experience; no criminal conviction for financial crimes or serious offences; no disqualification from serving as a director of any company; and no history of regulatory censure in the insurance or financial services sector.
Chair independence: The Board Chair must be a non-executive director. The Chair and MD/CEO roles must be held by different individuals to ensure the separation of oversight and management.

Sector expertise: The Board as a collective must have demonstrated competence in insurance or financial services, accounting and finance, legal matters, and corporate governance. NAICOM expects the Board to include at least one director with direct insurance industry experience.

blocks.h: NIIRA 2025 and best-practice governance standards require a Nigerian life insurer’s Board to maintain four principal committees, each with its own terms of reference, composition requirements, and reporting obligations:

rows: Committee
Composition
Core Mandate
Key Outputs
Audit Committee
Minimum three non-executive directors; chaired by an independent director with financial expertise; the external auditor attends by invitation.

Oversee the integrity of the financial statements; review the external audit process; oversee internal audit function independence and effectiveness; review compliance with NAICOM financial reporting requirements.
Approval of annual financial statements; recommendation of external auditor appointment to shareholders; internal audit reports; management letter follow-up.
Risk Committee
Minimum three non-executive directors; chaired by an independent director; the Chief Risk Officer is the primary management interface.
Review and approve the Risk Appetite Statement; oversee the ERM framework; review ORSA findings; monitor emerging risks; oversee the Statutory Actuary’s annual investigation findings.
Risk Appetite Statement; ORSA report review; emerging risk register; CRO quarterly risk dashboard.
Investment Committee

Mix of non-executive directors (including at least one with financial markets or investment expertise) and executive directors; the Chief Investment Officer/Finance Director is the primary management interface.
Approve and monitor the Investment Policy Statement; review portfolio performance against benchmarks and liability profile; oversee ALM strategy; approve investment in new asset classes.
Approved IPS; quarterly investment performance reports; ALM gap analysis; approval of strategic asset allocation changes.
Remuneration Committee
Majority non-executive directors; chaired by an independent director; no executive director may be present when their own remuneration is discussed.

Set remuneration policy for the Board and senior management; ensure remuneration is aligned with long-term performance and does not incentivise excessive risk-taking; oversee the company’s total compensation framework.
Board remuneration policy; CEO and executive team remuneration; remuneration report in the annual accounts; incentive scheme design approval.

blocks.text: 34.2.3 The MD/CEO and the Executive Committee

blocks.h: The Managing Director/Chief Executive Officer (MD/CEO) is the most senior executive of the company and is accountable to the Board for the overall management of the business: implementing the Board’s strategic direction, managing the company’s operations, achieving the agreed financial targets, maintaining regulatory compliance, and building the management team required to execute the strategy.

The Executive Committee (ExCo) is the primary management decision-making forum, chaired by the MD/CEO and comprising the heads of the principal functional areas of the business. In a well-structured Nigerian life insurer, the ExCo should include: the CFO/Finance Director; the Chief Risk Officer (CRO); the Chief Actuary/Statutory Actuary; the Chief Operations Officer; the Chief Distribution Officer; the Chief Marketing Officer; the Chief Technology Officer; the Head of Human Resources; and the Head of Legal and Compliance. The ExCo meets regularly (typically weekly or fortnightly) to manage the business’s day-to-day and near-term strategic priorities, escalating material issues to the Board.

blocks.text: 34.3 The Twelve Core Departments: Mandates and Activities

blocks.h: The Actuarial and Risk department is the technical heart of a life insurance company. It is responsible for the mathematical modelling of risk: pricing the products that the company sells, reserving for the liabilities those products create, assessing the company’s overall risk profile, and advising the Board and management on the adequacy of capital.

rows: Statutory Actuary

The NIIRA 2025-required Statutory Actuary is a Fellow of the Institute and Faculty of Actuaries (or equivalent) who certifies the annual actuarial investigation. The Statutory Actuary has a direct reporting line to the Board (not solely to the MD/CEO) to ensure independence. They sign the actuarial certificate that is filed with NAICOM as part of the annual statutory return.
Product pricing

Developing the premium basis for each new product: the mortality assumption, the investment return assumption, the expense loading, and the profit margin. Pricing models are validated by the Statutory Actuary and approved by the Board’s Risk Committee before products are filed with NAICOM.
Reserving

Calculating the life policy reserves, the outstanding claims reserves, the IBNR provision, and other technical provisions required under NIIRA 2025 and IFRS 17. Reserves must be adequate to meet all future policyholder obligations; under-reserving is a regulatory breach and a solvency risk.
ORSA (Own Risk and Solvency Assessment)

Producing the annual ORSA report that the Board must approve and submit to NAICOM. The ORSA assesses the company’s risk profile, its capital adequacy under stress scenarios, and the adequacy of its ERM framework.
ERM oversight

Maintaining the company’s Enterprise Risk Management framework; identifying, assessing, and monitoring all material risks across the business; and providing the Board’s Risk Committee with a comprehensive risk dashboard.
Profit source analysis

Analysing the four profit sources (mortality, interest, expense, and lapse) to identify which aspects of each product’s performance are generating or eroding value. Essential input for product management and pricing decisions.

blocks.h: The Underwriting department is responsible for assessing and accepting or declining individual risk: evaluating each application for life insurance coverage and deciding the terms on which the company is prepared to provide cover. Good underwriting is the foundation of a profitable life insurance book; poor underwriting generates adverse selection and claim losses that no pricing model can compensate for.

items.h: New business vetting: Reviewing all individual life applications above the non-medical limit; requesting medical evidence; assessing financial justification for high sum assureds; and applying the mortality table to each risk profile to determine the appropriate premium basis (standard, rated, or declined).

Medical underwriting: Interpreting medical evidence (doctor’s reports, blood tests, specialist reports) to assess the mortality implications of disclosed health conditions and determine the appropriate rating.
Group acceptance: Assessing and quoting group life schemes; setting free cover limits; reviewing census data; monitoring group schemes’ ongoing experience; and managing the renewal rating process.

Reinsurance placement: Ceding individual large-sum risks to the reinsurer under the retention limits agreed in the treaty; maintaining records of cessions; and managing the relationship with the reinsurance broker.

blocks.h: The Claims department is responsible for assessing and settling valid claims promptly and fairly, within NIIRA 2025’s mandatory settlement timelines. It is the department most directly responsible for the company’s reputation: a claims department that settles valid claims promptly and compassionately is the insurer’s most powerful retention and referral tool; one that delays, disputes, and declines legitimate claims is the insurer’s most damaging brand liability.

items.h: Individual life claims: Receiving and acknowledging death claim notifications; requesting the required documentation; assessing the claim against the policy terms; and settling valid claims within the NIIRA 2025 mandatory period.

Group life claims: Managing death and disability claims under employer group life schemes; coordinating with employers for required employment documentation; managing multiple simultaneous claims from large-scheme fatalities.

Fraud investigation: Identifying claims that exhibit fraud indicators (inconsistent documentation, cause of death discrepancies, multiple policies on the same life, early claims on recently issued policies); referring suspected fraudulent claims to the Special Investigation Unit (SIU); and coordinating with law enforcement where criminal fraud is suspected.

Contested claims and legal management: Managing claims that are in dispute; coordinating with the Legal team on contested claims that proceed to formal dispute resolution; and reporting NAICOM-required data on the claims settlement record.

blocks.h: The Sales and Distribution department is the company’s revenue engine. It manages all the channels through which the insurer reaches its customers: the tied agency force, bancassurance partnerships, corporate sales, broker relationships, and digital channels. The distribution function is typically the largest department by headcount and the largest single item in the company’s cost base (through agent commission).

items.h: Agency management: Recruiting, contracting, training, licensing (CIIN certification compliance), activating, and retaining the tied agent force. Setting production targets, monitoring performance, and managing the commission payment process.

Bancassurance: Managing the relationships with bancassurance partner banks: negotiating commercial terms, training bank staff, monitoring sales performance, and ensuring the insurer’s product is appropriately positioned in the bank’s product range.
Corporate and group sales: Direct sales of group life, group health, and employee benefit products to corporate employers; managing the corporate client relationship from tender to renewal.

Digital sales channel: Managing the insurer’s digital distribution infrastructure: the mobile app, USSD platform, and Insurtech partnership relationships. Digital channel performance monitoring and CAC optimisation.

blocks.h: The Marketing and Communications department is responsible for building the brand, generating demand for the insurer’s products, and communicating the company’s value to all stakeholder groups. In the Nigerian insurance market, where the trust deficit is the primary barrier to purchase, marketing’s most important function is not generating leads but building the brand credibility that makes every sales interaction more productive.

items.h: Brand management: Developing and protecting the company’s brand identity: the visual identity, the brand voice, the brand positioning (what the company stands for in the minds of its target customers), and the brand experience across all customer touchpoints.

Product marketing: Translating actuarial product features into customer-facing value propositions; developing product collateral; designing the product’s pricing presentation for each distribution channel; and managing product launch campaigns.

Digital marketing: Managing the company’s social media presence, content marketing, search engine optimisation, and digital lead generation; analysing the digital marketing funnel and optimising CAC across digital channels.

Public relations and corporate communications: Managing media relationships; overseeing press releases and public statements; managing crisis communications; and building the company’s reputation with regulatory, investor, and community stakeholders.

blocks.h: The Operations and Technology department is responsible for the internal machinery that makes the insurer’s business processes work: the Policy Administration System (PAS) that holds all policyholder records, the core banking and payment systems, the digital infrastructure, and the process design and improvement capability. In a market where digital transformation is reshaping distribution and servicing, the Operations and Technology function is increasingly a strategic differentiator, not merely a cost centre.

items.h: Policy Administration System (PAS) management: Maintaining the accuracy and availability of the PAS, which holds all policy records, premium transaction history, claims records, and beneficiary information. The PAS is the insurer’s most critical operational system; its failure, corruption, or cyber-compromise would be an operational catastrophe.

Process design and improvement: Mapping, documenting, and continuously improving the core business processes: policy issuance, premium collection, claims notification, policy servicing. Reducing processing time and error rates in core processes is the primary operational efficiency lever.
IT governance: Managing the IT asset base, cybersecurity, business continuity and disaster recovery planning, data governance (in compliance with NDPA 2023), and technology vendor relationships.

blocks.h: The Finance and Investment department is responsible for the insurer’s financial management: accounting, reporting, budgeting, investment management, and the filing of NAICOM’s statutory financial returns. It is led by the CFO, who is a key member of the Executive Committee and the primary interface with the Board’s Audit Committee and Investment Committee.

items.h: Premium accounting: Recording premium income, matching premiums to policies, reconciling premium receipts against expected billings, and managing the premium debtor book. Premium reconciliation accuracy is a critical operational control: unreconciled premium gaps create both financial reporting inaccuracies and potential coverage disputes.

Investment management: Managing the insurer’s investment portfolio within the Board-approved Investment Policy Statement and NAICOM’s admissible asset framework. Optimising yield while managing duration, credit, and liquidity risk in alignment with the ALM requirements of the insurer’s liability profile.

NAICOM statutory reporting: Preparing and filing the quarterly and annual statutory returns required by NAICOM: the financial returns, the solvency margin certificates, the actuarial return, and the market conduct returns. Timely and accurate statutory reporting is a basic regulatory compliance obligation.

Financial planning and budgeting: Developing the annual budget and multi-year financial projections; monitoring financial performance against budget; and providing management with the financial information needed for strategic decision-making.

blocks.h: The Legal and Compliance department is the insurer’s regulatory interface and legal risk manager. In the post-NIIRA 2025 environment, with expanded NAICOM powers, NDPA 2023 data protection obligations, MLPPA 2022 AML/CFT requirements, and an active market conduct supervisory framework, the Legal and Compliance function has moved from a peripheral advisory role to a central governance obligation.

items.h: Regulatory liaison: Managing the company’s relationship with NAICOM, PenCom (for annuity activities), NHIA (for health insurance), the CBN (for bancassurance regulatory interface), and other relevant regulators. Monitoring regulatory developments and representing the company in industry consultations.

Contract review: Reviewing all material contracts: distribution agreements, bancassurance arrangements, technology and outsourcing contracts, reinsurance treaties, and professional services agreements. Ensuring contracts adequately protect the company’s interests and comply with applicable law.

AML/KYC compliance: Implementing and maintaining the Anti-Money Laundering and Know Your Customer programme required under the Money Laundering (Prevention and Prohibition) Act 2022; filing the Suspicious Activity Reports required by the Financial Intelligence Unit.

NDPA 2023 data protection compliance: Ensuring all personal data collected from policyholders, claimants, agents, and employees is processed in accordance with the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023; maintaining the data audit trail; responding to data subject access requests; and managing any data breach notification obligations.

blocks.h: The Human Resources department is responsible for acquiring, developing, and retaining the talent the organisation needs to execute its strategy. In the Nigerian insurance market (where the talent pool for actuaries, investment professionals, digital specialists, and experienced underwriters is thin) the HR function is a strategic capability, not merely an administrative support.

items.h: Talent acquisition: Recruiting for all roles across the organisation; managing the employer brand; maintaining relationships with universities and professional bodies (CIIN, ICAN, CIMA); and managing the graduate trainee and internship programmes.

Training and development: Designing and delivering the technical training programmes for agents (CIIN Certificate of Proficiency compliance), technical insurance training for underwriters and claims staff, and the leadership development programmes for management. Managing the CIIN CPD compliance tracking for all professional staff.

Performance management: Designing and implementing the company’s performance management system: KPI frameworks by role, mid-year and annual appraisal processes, performance improvement plans, and the link between performance and compensation.

CIIN CPD compliance: Under NIIRA 2025, all insurance professionals must meet CIIN CPD requirements. HR is responsible for tracking CPD compliance across all relevant staff, ensuring the company’s training programme generates sufficient CPD credit hours, and reporting CPD compliance status to management.

blocks.h: The Customer Experience (CX) department is responsible for designing and delivering the experience that policyholders, prospective customers, and claimants have at every touchpoint with the insurer. In a market where customer trust is the primary determinant of insurance purchase and renewal, CX is not a supplementary function but a core strategic capability.

items.h: CX design: Mapping the customer journey across all touchpoints (from the first brand awareness moment through product selection, application, onboarding, premium payment, policy servicing, and claim settlement) identifying moments of friction and moments of delight, and designing processes and communications to maximise the positive experience at each stage.

Contact centre management: Operating the insurer’s inbound and outbound customer service function: handling policyholder queries, complaints, and requests; managing service level agreements (SLAs) for call response time and resolution; and routing complex or sensitive matters to the appropriate specialist team.

Conservation: Identifying policyholders at risk of lapsing and intervening proactively to conserve the policy: outreach to lapse-risk policyholders (using the lapse prediction model described in Chapter 28); premium reinstatement facilitation; product substitution where the original product no longer meets the policyholder’s needs; and complaint resolution.

blocks.h: The Strategy and Research department provides the intelligence and analytical framework for the company’s strategic decision-making. It is the department that answers the questions that the operational departments are too busy to ask: where is the market going? what are competitors doing? which products are winning and which are losing? what does the regulatory horizon look like? Chapter 27 (Strategy and Research Function) addressed this department’s mandate, research methods, and outputs in detail; it sits within the Actuarial and Risk function in smaller companies and as an independent function in larger ones.

Internal Audit is the insurer’s independent assurance function. It provides the Board’s Audit Committee with an objective assessment of whether the company’s internal controls, risk management processes, and governance arrangements are operating effectively. Critically, Internal Audit is independent of management: it reports directly to the Board’s Audit Committee, not to the CEO or CFO. This independence is mandated by NIIRA 2025 and is the foundational condition for genuine audit effectiveness.

items.h: Three lines of defence role: Internal Audit is the third line of defence in the NIIRA 2025-mandated three lines of defence model. The first line (management and operational teams) owns and manages risk day-to-day; the second line (Risk and Compliance functions) designs the risk framework and monitors compliance; the third line (Internal Audit) independently assesses whether the first two lines are operating effectively.

Audit programme: Developing a risk-based annual audit plan approved by the Audit Committee; executing audits of all material business processes, control systems, and risk management activities; and reporting findings and recommendations to the Audit Committee.

NAICOM and Board reporting: Providing the Audit Committee with quarterly audit reports; ensuring NAICOM’s market conduct inspections are supported with complete and accurate documentation; and following up management’s implementation of audit recommendations within agreed timelines.

blocks.text: 34.4 The Three Lines of Defence Model

blocks.title: The Three Lines of Defence in a Nigerian Life Insurer

blocks.h: FIRST LINE: OPERATIONAL MANAGEMENT (OWNS AND MANAGES RISK):

All business functions that directly own and execute the insurer’s activities: Underwriting, Claims, Sales, Finance, Operations, HR, and Marketing. The first line is responsible for implementing controls, identifying risks within its own processes, and managing those risks to within the agreed risk appetite. A claims manager who identifies a fraud risk in the claims process owns that risk; it is their first-line responsibility to control it, escalate it, and report it.
SECOND LINE: RISK AND COMPLIANCE FUNCTIONS (DESIGN THE FRAMEWORK AND MONITOR):

The Risk Management function (including the CRO and Actuarial team for insurance risk) and the Compliance function. The second line does not own the risks of the first-line functions, it designs the ERM framework within which those functions operate, monitors compliance with the framework, and escalates to the Board where first-line risk management is inadequate. The second line’s independence from the first line is essential: a CRO who reports to the same functional head as the underwriting team cannot provide independent risk oversight.
THIRD LINE: INTERNAL AUDIT (INDEPENDENT ASSURANCE):

The Internal Audit function provides the Board with independent assurance that the first and second lines are operating as intended. Internal Audit has no management responsibility for the risks or controls it audits; it assesses them objectively. Its direct reporting line to the Board’s Audit Committee is the structural guarantee of its independence. The external auditor (who signs the statutory financial statements) is sometimes described as a ‘fourth line’, providing independent assurance to shareholders and NAICOM beyond the internal assurance hierarchy.

blocks.text: 34.5 Recommended Organisational Models by Company Size

blocks.h: The appropriate organisational structure for a life insurance company depends fundamentally on its scale: the number of policies in force, the number of employees, the geographic footprint, the number of distribution channels, and the product range. A start-up insurer with 50 employees and 10,000 policies needs a different structure from a large composite with 800 employees and 500,000 policies. Applying a large-company structure to a small company creates bureaucratic overhead that kills agility; applying a start-up structure to a large company creates governance gaps that NIIRA 2025 will not tolerate.

blocks.text: 34.5.1 The Start-Up Life Insurer (fewer than 100 employees)

blocks.h: STRUCTURAL IMPERATIVE: Functional breadth with role combination. At start-up scale, the insurer cannot afford the full department structure of a large company. Every manager must cover multiple functions, and departments must be combined where the workload does not yet justify standalone teams.

Recommended reporting structure: All functions report to the MD/CEO directly (flat hierarchy). The MD/CEO’s immediate direct reports typically include: a combined CFO/Compliance Head; the Statutory Actuary (who also covers risk); a combined Underwriting/Claims Head; the Head of Sales; and the Head of Operations (who also covers technology and HR). Total ExCo: 5–6 members.

Non-negotiable functions that cannot be combined: The Statutory Actuary and Internal Audit Head must be genuinely independent of the functions they oversee, even at start-up scale. A part-time or outsourced Internal Audit Head reporting directly to the Audit Committee is preferable to no internal audit function.

Growth trigger: When the company reaches approximately 50–75 employees and 50,000 policies in force, the functional combination model begins to strain. This is the signal to begin separating combined functions into dedicated departments, starting with Risk (separating from Actuarial), Compliance (separating from Finance), and HR (separating from Operations).

At mid-size scale, the insurer has enough volume and complexity to justify separate departments for each core function, but not yet the scale to support deep specialist teams within each department. The mid-size structure is typically functional: each department head owns their function completely and reports to a member of the ExCo or directly to the MD/CEO.

Recommended ExCo composition: MD/CEO; CFO; CRO; Chief Actuary; Chief Distribution Officer; COO; Head of Legal and Compliance. Department heads for Marketing, HR, CX, and IT report to one of the ExCo members (not directly to the MD/CEO), creating a two-tier management structure that preserves management bandwidth at the top while ensuring accountability at the functional level.

At mid-size, the critical structural investment is in the second-line functions. Many Nigerian insurers at this scale have an adequate first line (operational departments that process business) but an inadequate second line (a nominal Risk function that does not genuinely monitor or challenge the first line). This is the governance gap that NIIRA 2025’s three lines of defence requirement is designed to close.

At large-company scale, the insurer faces different organisational challenges: coordination across large specialist teams, management of complex matrix dependencies (a product development initiative simultaneously involves Actuarial, Underwriting, Marketing, Legal, and Operations), and the risk of silo formation, departments that optimise their own function at the expense of cross-functional effectiveness.

The large composite typically employs a hybrid structure: functional departments for core specialist activities (Actuarial, Underwriting, Claims, Finance, Legal) combined with customer-facing or product-based business units that cut across the functional silos. For example, a separate Corporate EB Business Unit might have its own sales team, account management, and product specialists, drawing on centralised Actuarial, Legal, and Compliance services from the functional departments.

At this scale, the Span of Control principle becomes critical: each manager should have no more than 6–8 direct reports for roles requiring close supervision, and no more than 10–12 for more routine roles. A department head with 25 direct reports cannot provide genuine management or development to any of them; the team’s effective management requires an additional layer of team leaders or managers.

The choice between a functional structure (in which each employee belongs to a single functional department and reports to that department’s head) and a matrix structure (in which an employee has two reporting lines, a functional reporting line and a project or business unit reporting line) is one of the most consequential organisational design decisions a growing insurer faces.

rows: Dimension
Functional Structure
Matrix Structure
Clarity of authority
Clear: each employee has one line manager. Accountability is unambiguous.
Complex: dual reporting creates potential confusion about which manager’s instructions take priority.
Specialist depth
High: specialists are grouped with their peers, sharing knowledge and developing expertise.
Variable: specialists are deployed across projects, which broadens experience but may dilute depth.
Cross-functional coordination
Weak: departments tend to optimise their own function; cross-functional projects require senior management mediation.
Strong: the matrix design explicitly creates cross-functional collaboration pathways, though at the cost of structural complexity.
Speed of decision-making
Moderate: decisions within a department are fast; decisions requiring cross-departmental input are slow (require escalation to the common superior).
Potentially faster for cross-functional decisions if the matrix is well-designed; potentially slower if the dual reporting creates decision gridlock.
Best suited for
Start-ups and mid-size insurers with clear functional boundaries; companies where specialist depth is the primary competitive advantage.
Large companies managing multiple product lines or distribution channels simultaneously; insurers pursuing complex transformational projects.
Nigerian insurance context
The dominant model in the Nigerian market. Appropriate for the majority of Nigerian life insurers at their current scale.
Appropriate for large composites and for specific project-based work (IFRS 17 implementation, digital transformation programmes). Pure matrix is rarely effective in the Nigerian context.

blocks.h: The twelve departments described in Section 34.3 do not operate as independent units. They are connected by flows of information, shared decisions, and mutual dependencies that must be actively managed through structured integration mechanisms. The most commercially critical integration points are:

The most important feedback loop in any life insurance operation is the flow of claims experience data from the Claims department to the Underwriting team. Underwriting decides which risks to accept and at what terms; Claims discovers, months or years later, whether those decisions were correct. An Underwriting team that never sees claims experience data cannot improve its risk selection; a Claims team that cannot communicate emerging adverse experience to Underwriting is unable to prevent its recurrence.

Best-practice integration: monthly claims experience reports distributed to Underwriting; a joint Underwriting-Claims review of each year’s claims against the year’s underwriting decisions; and a defined escalation path for Underwriting to raise concerns about specific risk categories with Claims without waiting for the annual review.

Sales teams are under constant commercial pressure to reduce premiums, offer broader coverage, relax underwriting requirements, and match competitors’ terms. Actuarial teams are under professional obligation to price risks accurately and maintain adequate reserves. The tension between these objectives is healthy, a company that never reduces premiums misses growth; a company that always reduces premiums destroys profitability.

Best-practice integration: a Product Pricing Committee that includes both Sales leadership and the Chief Actuary, meeting quarterly, to review premium adequacy for each product line and agree pricing changes based on both competitive intelligence and actuarial analysis. The Pricing Committee’s decisions are a shared commitment, not a concession by either function.

A product that actuaries design without marketing input may be technically sound but fail in the market because it does not address a genuine consumer need in a way consumers understand. A product that marketing designs without actuarial input may be commercially appealing but impossible to price profitably. The product development process must be inherently cross-functional: consumer insight from Research and Marketing, benefit design from Actuarial, distribution feasibility from Sales, and compliance sign-off from Legal.

The six-gate product innovation process described in Chapter 27 is the structural solution to this integration requirement: gates owned by different functions, with no gate advancing without sign-off from all relevant departments.

The Operations function designs the business processes; the Technology function builds and maintains the systems that automate those processes. When these two functions are misaligned (Operations designing processes without understanding system constraints, or Technology building systems without understanding operational requirements) the result is either systems that do not match the process (requiring manual workarounds) or processes that are redesigned to fit the system’s limitations (rather than the customer’s needs).

Best-practice integration: a joint Operations-Technology steering committee that manages the insurer’s system change programme; a defined change management process through which new business requirements are translated into system specifications; and a shared SLA framework that holds Technology accountable for system availability and Operations accountable for process compliance.

The Board Charter (or Board Terms of Reference) is the foundational governance document that defines the Board’s role, authority, composition, meeting requirements, and relationship with management. It codifies the distinction between governance (the Board’s domain) and management (the CEO’s domain), and defines the matters reserved for Board decision versus those delegated to management.

A well-drafted Board Charter under NIIRA 2025 should specify: the minimum number of directors and the independence requirements; the roles of the Chair and the MD/CEO and the prohibition on their combination; the matters specifically reserved for Board approval (strategy, annual budget, capital transactions, material acquisitions, regulatory filings, dividend decisions, and any transaction above a defined materiality threshold); the conduct of Board meetings (frequency, quorum, voting procedures); and the Board evaluation process.

The Delegation of Authority (DoA) is the document that maps the chain of financial and operational authority from the Board down through the ExCo to department heads and individual managers. It specifies: who can approve expenditure at each level (e.g., any manager up to ₦5 million, the CFO up to ₦50 million, the ExCo up to ₦200 million, the Board above ₦200 million); who can sign contracts on behalf of the company; who can approve claims above certain thresholds; and who can commit to reinsurance programmes.

The DoA is a critical internal control document: it prevents decisions being made by individuals without the authority to make them, and provides a clear framework for escalation when decisions exceed an individual’s authority level. A company without a current, complete DoA is operating without a foundational internal control, and is likely in breach of NIIRA 2025’s governance requirements.

The Conflict of Interest Policy defines what constitutes a conflict of interest for directors, executives, and employees; the obligation to disclose conflicts when they arise; and the process for managing disclosed conflicts (typically, the conflicted individual recuses themselves from the relevant discussion and decision). In the Nigerian insurance market, where business relationships are often personal as well as commercial, the Conflict of Interest Policy is essential for maintaining the integrity of procurement, underwriting, claims, and investment decisions.

The Code of Conduct sets the behavioural standards expected of all directors, executives, and employees of the insurer: honesty and integrity in all business dealings; compliance with applicable law and regulation; respect for policyholders, colleagues, and business partners; protection of confidential information; responsible use of company assets; and the obligation to report suspected breaches. The Code of Conduct is the cultural anchor of the governance framework, it translates the governance structure’s formal requirements into the day-to-day behaviours expected of every person in the organisation.

blocks.text: 34.9 Advisory: Building the Well-Governed Nigerian Life Insurer

blocks.h: Organisational design is not a one-time exercise. A company’s structure should evolve continuously as the business grows, as the regulatory environment changes, and as the competitive landscape shifts. The most common organisational failures in Nigerian life insurers are not dramatic collapses; they are slow accumulations of structural inadequacy: a Risk function that was never given the authority to challenge management; a Claims team that was too small relative to the claims volume; an IT function that was too junior to have genuine influence over the insurer’s technology direction.

blocks.title: Advisory: Six Organisational Design Principles for the Post-NIIRA 2025 Nigerian Life Insurer

blocks.h: PRINCIPLE 1: STRUCTURE FOLLOWS STRATEGY, NOT CONVENTION. There is no single correct structure for a life insurer. The structure should reflect the specific competitive position the insurer is pursuing: an insurer committed to a digital-first mass market strategy needs a Technology function that reports to the CEO, not a Finance Director; an insurer focused on the corporate EB market needs a senior corporate sales leadership, not a field agent management hierarchy. Structure the organisation for the strategy you are executing, not for the industry template.

PRINCIPLE 2: RESOURCE THE SECOND LINE ADEQUATELY. The most common structural deficiency in Nigerian life insurers is an under-resourced second line. A Risk function of one junior analyst and a Compliance function of one administrative officer cannot credibly oversee the risk and compliance dimensions of a company with 200 employees and ₦50 billion in premium income. The second line requires qualified professionals, genuine independence, and direct access to the Board. If the second line cannot say ‘no’ to management and make it stick, it is not a second line; it is a reporting function.

PRINCIPLE 3: INVEST IN THE STATUTORY ACTUARY ROLE. The Statutory Actuary is not a signature on a regulatory form. They are the professional whose opinion on reserve adequacy, pricing soundness, and risk capital is the Board’s primary actuarial check on management. An insurer whose Statutory Actuary is a part-time consultant who attends one Board meeting a year and signs the annual return without ongoing involvement in pricing and reserving decisions is not meeting the spirit of NIIRA 2025’s actuarial requirements.

PRINCIPLE 4: SEPARATE THE CHAIR AND MD/CEO ROLES CLEARLY. In many Nigerian companies, the Chair and CEO roles are occupied by individuals with such close personal and professional relationships that the Board’s independence from management is nominal rather than real. A Chair who defers to the CEO on every governance question, approves every management recommendation without challenge, and attends Board meetings as a formality is not providing the oversight that shareholders and NAICOM require.

PRINCIPLE 5: DOCUMENT THE GOVERNANCE FRAMEWORK COMPLETELY. A Board Charter, Delegation of Authority, Conflict of Interest Policy, and Code of Conduct that exist as current, approved, and annually reviewed documents are the minimum governance infrastructure required by NIIRA 2025. Many Nigerian insurers have these documents in draft or outdated form; NAICOM’s supervisory team will request them at any market conduct inspection.

PRINCIPLE 6: INTEGRATE DELIBERATELY. The twelve departments described in this chapter will not integrate naturally. Left to their own devices, departments optimise their own metrics and minimise their obligations to other functions. The integration mechanisms (joint committees, shared KPIs, structured cross-functional processes, and ExCo-sponsored collaboration) must be deliberately designed and actively maintained by the MD/CEO and the ExCo.

blocks.title: The Single Most Important Structural Investment for a Nigerian Life Insurer

blocks.h: A Chief Risk Officer with the seniority, independence, and Board access to genuinely challenge management’s risk decisions is the single most valuable structural investment a Nigerian life insurer can make in the post-NIIRA 2025 environment. Not because NAICOM requires it, which it does, but because the commercial risks of under-pricing, adverse selection, excessive lapse rates, and investment concentration that destroy insurance companies are all risks that a well-empowered CRO would identify and escalate before they become business-threatening. The insurer that treats the CRO role as a compliance checkbox will eventually discover the cost of that decision in its claims experience, its solvency position, or its regulatory enforcement history.

The apex governance body of a Nigerian life insurance company, accountable to shareholders for the oversight of strategy, risk management, financial performance, and regulatory compliance; composed under NIIRA 2025 requirements for a majority of non-executive directors and minimum independent directors.
A Board member who does not have an executive management role in the company; provides independent oversight of management and chairs or sits on Board committees.
A non-executive director with no material relationship to the company, its major shareholders, or its management; required to chair the Audit and Risk Committees under NIIRA 2025.

NAICOM’s requirements for directors and key management personnel: adequate qualifications or experience, no criminal conviction for relevant offences, no history of regulatory censure, and no disqualification from directorship.
The primary management decision-making forum of the insurer, chaired by the MD/CEO and comprising the heads of principal functional areas.

The governance model mandated by NIIRA 2025 in which: the first line (operational management) owns and manages risk; the second line (Risk and Compliance) designs the framework and monitors; and the third line (Internal Audit) provides independent assurance.
A Fellow of a recognised actuarial institute appointed under NIIRA 2025 requirements to certify the annual actuarial investigation, with a direct reporting line to the Board.

The senior executive responsible for the Enterprise Risk Management framework, the ORSA, and the monitoring of all material risks across the business; reports to the MD/CEO and has direct access to the Board’s Risk Committee.

The senior executive responsible for the insurer’s regulatory compliance programme, AML/KYC obligations, NDPA 2023 compliance, and the management of the regulatory relationship with NAICOM and other regulators.
The document mapping financial and operational approval authority from the Board through the ExCo to department heads and individual managers.
The foundational governance document defining the Board’s role, composition, authority, meeting requirements, and relationship with management; includes the matters reserved for Board decision.
The document defining what constitutes a conflict of interest, the obligation to disclose conflicts, and the process for managing disclosed conflicts through recusal.
The behavioural standards document expected of all directors, executives, and employees, covering honesty, compliance, respect, confidentiality, and the obligation to report breaches.
An organisational design in which each employee belongs to a single functional department and reports to that department’s head; dominant in Nigerian life insurance.
An organisational design in which employees have dual reporting lines, functional and project or business unit, enabling cross-functional collaboration at the cost of greater structural complexity.
The number of direct reports managed by a single manager; typically 6–8 for roles requiring close supervision and up to 10–12 for more routine roles.

items.h: Galbraith, J.R. Designing Organizations: An Executive Guide to Strategy, Structure, and Process (Jossey-Bass, 2002). The definitive reference for organisational design; functional vs. matrix structures and integration mechanisms.
Mintzberg, H. Structure in Fives: Designing Effective Organizations (Prentice Hall, 1992). Classic organisational theory; spans of control, coordination mechanisms, and structural configurations.

Goold, M. and Campbell, A. Designing Effective Organizations (Jossey-Bass, 2002). Practical application of organisational design principles to large corporations; relevant to large composite insurer design.

King IV Report on Corporate Governance. iodsa.co.za. The South African King IV Report is the most relevant African governance reference for financial institutions; widely referenced by Nigerian governance practitioners.
OECD. Principles of Corporate Governance. oecd.org. The global baseline governance reference.
IIF (Institute of International Finance). ‘Governance Reform in Financial Institutions.’ iif.com.

IAIS. Insurance Core Principles, Standards, Guidance and Assessment Methodology. iaisweb.org. ICP 7 (Corporate Governance) and ICP 8 (Risk Management and Internal Controls) are the primary global references for insurance governance standards.
LOMA. ‘Governance and Management of Life Insurance Companies.’ FLMI Programme. loma.org.
PwC. ‘Insurance Governance: Aligning Boards with Regulatory Expectations.’ pwc.com.

Nigerian Insurance Industry Reform Act (NIIRA) 2025 (Act No. 2, 2025). Corporate governance provisions; Board composition; fit and proper requirements; three lines of defence; Statutory Actuary; Chief Risk Officer; Chief Compliance Officer. naicom.gov.ng.
NAICOM. Prudential Guidelines for Insurance Companies. naicom.gov.ng.
Financial Reporting Council of Nigeria (FRC). Nigerian Code of Corporate Governance 2018. frcnigeria.gov.ng.
Companies and Allied Matters Act (CAMA) 2020. Board composition, director duties, and company secretarial requirements.
